The layered structure and the rheological properties of anti-wear films, generated in a rolling/sliding contact from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and/or molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC) additives, have been studied by dynamic nanoindentation experiments coupled with a simple modelling of the stiffness measurements. Local nano-friction experiments were conducted with the same device in order to determine the evolution of the friction coefficient as a function of the applied pressure for the different lubricant formulations. For the MoDTC film, the applied pressure in the friction test remains low (<0.5 GPa) and the apparent friction coefficient is high ($\mu$ > 0.4). For the tribofilms containing MoDTC together with ZDTP, which permits the applied pressure to increase up to a few GPa through some accommodation process, a very low friction domain appears (0.01 < $\mu$ < 0.05), located a few nanometers below the surface of the tribofilm. This low friction coefficient is attributed to the presence of MoS2 planes sliding over each other in a favourable configuration obtained when the pressure is sufficiently high, which is made possible by the presence of ZDTP.

# Investigation of Anti-Wear Film Structure and Friction Behavior in ZDTP and MoDTC Lubricant Additives

The layered structure and rheological properties of anti-wear films derived from ZDTP (zinc dialkyldithiophosphate) and MoDTC (molybdenum dithiocarbamate) lubricant additives were investigated using dynamic nanoindentation experiments combined with stiffness measurement modelling. This experimental approach enabled a detailed characterization of the mechanical response of the tribofilms at the nanoscale, providing insight into their internal composition and depth-dependent properties.

To complement the structural analysis, local nano-friction experiments were performed to determine how the friction coefficient evolves as a function of applied pressure across different lubricant formulations. By systematically varying the contact conditions, it was possible to establish the relationship between mechanical loading and frictional performance for each additive system.

The results revealed distinct behaviors depending on the additive composition. The MoDTC-only film exhibited a high apparent friction coefficient (μ > 0.4) and could sustain only relatively low applied pressures, remaining below 0.5 GPa. This indicates that, in isolation, the MoDTC-derived film lacks the mechanical robustness necessary to support higher contact loads while maintaining low friction.

In contrast, tribofilms formed from a combination of MoDTC and ZDTP demonstrated markedly superior performance. These composite films allowed applied pressures to reach several GPa and, crucially, produced a very low friction domain (0.01 < μ < 0.05) located a few nanometers below the surface. The presence of this low-friction region highlights the synergistic interaction between the two additives.

The very low friction observed in the combined formulation is attributed to the sliding of MoS₂ planes over one another in a favourable crystallographic configuration. This favourable alignment is enabled by the higher pressures that the film can withstand, which are made possible by the mechanical support provided by ZDTP. In this way, the ZDTP component reinforces the tribofilm structure, allowing the intrinsic lubricating properties of the MoS₂ layers to be fully realized under demanding contact conditions.

# Investigating Anti-Wear Tribofilms Through Advanced Nanomechanical Characterization

Anti-wear films generated in rolling/sliding contacts play a crucial role in protecting mechanical components and reducing energy losses in lubricated systems. In this study, tribofilms formed from lubricants containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and/or molybdenum dithiocarbamate (MoDTC) additives were investigated using an integrated experimental approach. The methodology combined dynamic nanoindentation with stiffness modelling and localized nano-friction experiments, enabling detailed characterization of the films' layered structure and rheological properties as a function of applied pressure. This multi-technique strategy allowed researchers to probe the mechanical response of these tribofilms at the nanoscale, revealing how their behavior evolves with depth and loading conditions.

## Synergistic Effects of Combined Additives

The results demonstrated a striking difference between films formed from individual additives and those generated by the combined MoDTC/ZDTP formulation. The combined tribofilm exhibited a distinctive very low friction domain, with coefficients of friction ranging between 0.01 and 0.05, located just a few nanometers beneath the surface. This exceptional frictional performance was attributed to the presence of favourably oriented MoS₂ (molybdenum disulfide) planes within the film. Critically, this favourable orientation was made possible by the pressure-accommodating properties imparted by the ZDTP component of the tribofilm.

## Implications for Ultra-Low Friction Lubrication

These findings underscore the importance of additive synergy in achieving ultra-low friction performance. Neither additive alone could produce the same beneficial effect; rather, it was the combined action of both ZDTP and MoDTC that created the optimal conditions for low-friction behavior. The ZDTP-derived layer appears to provide a mechanically accommodating substructure that allows the MoS₂ sheets to align in orientations that minimize shear resistance. This work therefore demonstrates that the interplay between different lubricant additives is not merely additive but genuinely synergistic, and that understanding this cooperative behavior at the nanoscale is essential for the rational design of advanced lubricant formulations aimed at reducing friction and improving the efficiency and durability of mechanical systems.

# ZDDP and MoDTC: Essential Lubricant Additives

## Introduction

Modern engine oils rely on carefully balanced chemical additives to protect vital components and extend engine life. Two of the most important additives in this category are **ZDDP** (Zinc Dialkyl Dithiophosphate) and **MoDTC** (Molybdenum Dithiocarbamate). These compounds work individually and synergistically to reduce wear and friction inside internal combustion engines.

## What Is ZDDP?

Zinc Dialkyl Dithiophosphate has been a cornerstone anti-wear additive since the 1940s. Its primary functions include:

- **Anti-wear protection**: ZDDP forms a protective phosphate glass film on metal surfaces, preventing metal-to-metal contact under high pressure.
- **Antioxidant properties**: It helps neutralize harmful acids and peroxides that degrade oil over time.
- **Corrosion inhibition**: The film protects surfaces from chemical attack.

ZDDP is particularly valuable in protecting the valvetrain, camshafts, and other high-stress components.

## What Is MoDTC?

Molybdenum Dithiocarbamate is primarily used as a **friction modifier**. When exposed to heat and pressure, MoDTC decomposes to form molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), a solid lubricant with an exceptionally low coefficient of friction. Its main benefits include:

- **Reduced friction**: Lower friction improves fuel economy.
- **Enhanced efficiency**: Less energy is lost to internal resistance.
- **Wear reduction**: Complements anti-wear additives for smoother operation.

## The Synergy Between ZDDP and MoDTC

When used together, ZDDP and MoDTC create a powerful protective system. The tribofilm formed by their combination often outperforms either additive alone, delivering both **excellent wear protection** and **superior friction reduction**. This partnership is especially valuable in meeting modern fuel-efficiency standards without compromising durability.

## Challenges and Considerations

Despite their benefits, these additives face limitations:

- **Catalyst compatibility**: The phosphorus in ZDDP can poison catalytic converters over time, leading to reduced concentrations in modern formulations.
- **Environmental regulations**: Increasing pressure to reduce emissions has driven research into alternative additives.
- **Balancing act**: Formulators must carefully balance these compounds to optimize performance while meeting emission requirements.

## Conclusion

ZDDP and MoDTC remain fundamental to modern lubricant technology. Their combined ability to reduce wear and friction makes them indispensable for protecting engines and improving efficiency. As automotive technology evolves, ongoing research continues to refine their use and explore next-generation alternatives.

Zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC) are widely employed lubricant additives that function synergistically to reduce wear and friction in mechanical contacts. While their macroscopic tribological performance is well documented, the nanoscale mechanical and frictional properties of the tribofilms they generate remain incompletely understood. In this study, nanoindentation and nano-friction techniques were used to characterize anti-wear tribofilms formed from ZDTP and MoDTC additives, both individually and in combination, under boundary lubrication conditions. Tribofilms were generated on steel substrates using a reciprocating tribometer, and their surface morphology, hardness, elastic modulus, and local frictional response were investigated using atomic force microscopy (AFM) and instrumented nanoindentation.

The results reveal that ZDTP-derived films exhibit a characteristic pad-like structure with significant spatial heterogeneity in hardness and modulus, reflecting variations in film thickness and composition. The incorporation of MoDTC alters the film architecture and produces a low-shear-strength surface layer, attributed to the formation of molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), which markedly reduces the coefficient of friction at the nanoscale. Nano-friction measurements demonstrate a strong correlation between the presence of MoS₂-rich domains and localized friction reduction, while nanoindentation data indicate that the combined additive system maintains adequate load-bearing capacity and mechanical robustness. Depth-dependent measurements further reveal a graded mechanical structure, with a softer outer layer overlying a harder, phosphate-rich bulk film.

These findings provide insight into the structure–property relationships governing tribofilm behavior and highlight the synergistic mechanism by which ZDTP and MoDTC combine wear protection with friction reduction. The nanoscale characterization approach offers a valuable framework for the rational design of next-generation lubricant additive formulations.

# MoDTC and ZDDP Synergy in Low-Friction Tribofilm Formation

## Background on the Additives

**MoDTC (Molybdenum Dialkyldithiocarbamate)** is the primary friction-reducing additive, while **ZDTP/ZDDP (Zinc Dialkyldithiophosphate)** is principally an anti-wear and antioxidant additive. When combined, they produce a layered tribofilm structure with distinct functional domains.

## MoS₂ Plane Formation (The Low-Friction Mechanism)

The friction reduction from MoDTC originates from the **tribochemical decomposition** of the molybdenum-containing molecule under contact conditions:

- Under shear, heat, and pressure, MoDTC decomposes to form **molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂)** nanosheets.
- MoS₂ has a **lamellar (layered) crystal structure**, where strong covalent bonds exist *within* each S-Mo-S sheet, but only weak **van der Waals forces** exist *between* the sheets.
- These basal planes **slide easily over one another**, providing an extremely low coefficient of friction (typically ~0.04–0.07).
- The friction reduction depends on forming well-ordered, extended MoS₂ **basal planes oriented parallel to the sliding direction**.

## Role of ZDDP in Pressure Accommodation

ZDDP forms a **phosphate glass tribofilm** that serves a crucial supporting role:

- ZDDP generates a **polyphosphate/pyrophosphate glassy layer** on the metal surface (typically iron/zinc phosphate chains).
- This film is **mechanically robust and pressure-accommodating**—it deforms and distributes contact stresses.
- The phosphate matrix acts as a **compliant substrate** that supports the fragile MoS₂ nanosheets, preventing them from being crushed or rapidly worn away.

## The Synergistic Layered Domain

The combination produces a **functionally graded, stratified tribofilm**:

| Layer | Composition | Function |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| **Top/sliding interface** | MoS₂ nanosheets | Low-friction shear plane |
| **Substrate/anchoring layer** | ZDDP phosphate glass | Pressure accommodation, mechanical support |

### Key synergistic effects:

1. **Stress accommodation**: The phosphate glass absorbs and redistributes high contact pressures, allowing the MoS₂ platelets to remain intact and properly oriented rather than being fragmented.

2. **Adhesion and retention**: The phosphate underlayer helps **anchor** the MoS₂ domains to the surface, promoting continuous replenishment and durability of the low-friction phase.

3. **Optimized MoS₂ formation**: The chemical environment created by ZDDP decomposition can influence the sulfur availability and **tribochemistry**, affecting the balance of MoS₂ formation versus less-favorable molybdenum oxides.

## Practical Consideration

The relationship is **concentration-dependent**—excessive ZDDP can *antagonize* friction reduction by competing for surface sites or forming a thick phosphate film that hinders MoS₂ deposition. Optimal formulations balance the ratio so ZDDP provides mechanical support without smothering the MoS₂ low-friction domain.

---

**In summary**: MoDTC supplies the intrinsic **low-friction MoS₂ lamellar planes** via tribochemical decomposition, while ZDDP provides a **pressure-accommodating phosphate glass** that mechanically supports and stabilizes these sheets—together creating a durable, low-friction domain that neither additive achieves alone.

# Anti-Wear Film Structure and Tribological Properties

Anti-wear films generated within rolling/sliding contacts, most notably those derived from zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) additives, exhibit a characteristic heterogeneous, layered architecture that spans from the substrate interface to the outermost surface. Nanoscale characterization reveals a graded structure in which a thin, iron-rich reaction layer bonds intimately to the steel substrate, transitioning into a bulk pad region composed predominantly of amorphous zinc phosphate and polyphosphate glass. The degree of polymerization varies through the film thickness, with short-chain ortho- and pyrophosphates dominating near the substrate and longer-chain polyphosphates concentrated toward the surface, culminating in an organic-rich, sulphur-bearing outermost layer. These films typically develop as discontinuous, patchy pads several tens to hundreds of nanometres thick, separated by valleys, producing a spatially non-uniform coverage across the contact.

The mechanical and rheological response of these tribofilms is strongly depth-dependent, reflecting the compositional gradient. Nanoindentation and modulus mapping demonstrate elastic moduli ranging from approximately 30–90 GPa and hardness values of 1–7 GPa, with the stiffer, more highly cross-linked material located near the substrate and a comparatively compliant, viscoelastic character at the surface. This gradation enables the film to accommodate contact stresses through a combination of elastic deformation and localized plastic flow, while the polyphosphate network's capacity for chain-length rearrangement and cation exchange (e.g., digestion of abrasive iron oxides) underpins its self-healing and load-bearing behaviour under repeated stress cycling.

Locally resolved friction measurements, obtained via lateral force microscopy and colloidal-probe techniques, indicate that friction coefficients across the tribofilm are spatially variable and correlate with local composition, topography, and mechanical stiffness. Reported nanoscale friction coefficients typically fall in the range of ~0.10–0.15 under boundary lubrication conditions, though values are sensitive to contact pressure, sliding velocity, temperature, and the presence of interfacial shear layers. The pad regions generally exhibit higher and more variable friction than the surrounding valleys, and the outermost, less-polymerized layer may present a shear-accommodating interface that governs the effective frictional dissipation of the contact.
